entries.title: Opposition growing to CAS-ordered Russia ice hockey reinstatement
entries.summary: Ice hockey's world governing body says the impact of a court decision forcing it to reinstate Russia has been "significantly underestimated." Several leading nations say they won't play against Russian teams.
entries.content:
November 4, 2026

Ice hockey's world governing body says the impact of a court decision forcing it to reinstate Russia has been "significantly underestimated." Several leading nations say they won't play against Russian teams.

The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement on Wednesday that the impact of last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) decision requiring it to reinstate Russia to international play had been "significantly underestimated." 

It added that it "maintains" its disagreement with the decision and that it remained "in dialogue with Member National Associations, organizing committees, host authorities and other key stakeholders to determine the best way forward."

The statement comes after two days of talks by the IIHF Council aimed at charting a way forward following Friday's CAS decision, which appears to have caught most of the international ice hockey community off guard.

Two of the organizing committees the statement refers to are those of Canada, which is due to host the IIHF World Junior Championship starting next month and Germany, which is to host the IIHF Men's World Championship next May. Both countries are strong supporters of Ukraine in its war against Russia, and both have expressed serious reservations about their upcoming tournaments in light of the CAS ruling.

Shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the IIHF barred its teams from competing in international ice hockey tournaments, citing security concerns. In last Friday's ruling, the CAS said that the IIHF's concerns were "not supported by sufficient evidence."

'Russians will not be in Canada'

On Tuesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ruled out allowing Russians to compete in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified, ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he told reporters at a press conference in Antigua, where he was attending a Commonwealth meeting.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there," he said.

Last weekend, Frank Lutz, chairman of the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) conceded in a television interview that following the CAS decision, the DEB would "also have to consider the option of handing back (hosting rights to) this championship."

Lutz was to discuss the matter with government officials in Berlin this week. A government spokesman said on the weekend that Berlin "takes a very critical view" of the ruling.

Growing European boycott of Russia

Meanwhile, the ice hockey association of Finland, the defending men's world champions, have been spearheading an effort to boycott upcoming IIHF tournaments should the Russians be allowed to compete.

"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen said in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday.

"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.

Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Czechia have since made similar statements.  

"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson said.

This came shortly after Norway said it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.

"Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors.

Czechia Ice Hockey Association President Alois Hadamczik confirmed on Tuesday that they too would refrain from playing Russian teams.

Latvia's federation said it “reaffirms its longstanding and firm position" not to play against Russia or its ally Belarus.

Alexander Helwig, chairman of the Austrian Ice Hockey Association told public broadcaster ORF that “as of now, we would certainly not play against Russia."

USA Hockey has yet to comment on the CAS ruling.

Sponsors having second thoughts

At the same time, sponsors of IIHF tournaments are also getting cold feet. Skoda, which has been the main sponsor of the Men's World Championship for more than three decades told the Associated Press that it would "reassess" its position if Russia takes part.

"We do not support the Court of Arbitration for Sport's decision regarding the participation of Russian national teams in IIHF competitions. With Russia's aggression continuing, we believe the Russian national team's return to the world championship is incompatible with the values we have consistently upheld," the Czech carmaker said.

Skoda isn't alone either, Finnish tire manufacturer Nokian had said it would end its backing if Russia took part and Swedish furniture maker AJ Products, whose logo has been seen on the boards and officials' jerseys at World Championships since 1989, said Monday it would ask for its logo not to be shown.

With the IIHF Council having failed to agree on how to proceed during its meetings on Monday and Tuesday, President Franz Reindl told Germany's SID news agency on Wednesday, that it would reconvene for further talks on Thursday.

entries.title: Germany news: Commerce chief calls for stable US trade relations after midterms, warning that uncertainty over Trump's tariff policies remains
entries.summary: German business is pinning its hopes on greater stability in US trade relations after a midterm blow for Donald Trump. Meanwhile, Germany's automakers appear to be feeling less gloomy than in recent years. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Commerce chief hopes for more stable US trade

November 4, 2026

German business is pinning its hopes on greater stability in US trade relations after a midterm blow for Donald Trump. Meanwhile, Germany's automakers appear to be feeling less gloomy than in recent years. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Germany's main Chamber of Commerce says it's hoping for more predictable US trade policy after Donald Trump's Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress

  • Germany's auto industry confidence has jumped to its highest level since mid-2024, according to a survey

  • Despite the improvement, experts warn that uncertainty remains high and German carmakers still face major challenges

  • Housing giant Vonovia has criticized Berlin's proposed takeover of large private housing portfolios

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, November 4, 2026:

Skip next section German commerce chief urges US tariff stability

German commerce chief urges US tariff stability

The head of Germany's main Chamber of Commerce has called for more predictable US trade policy after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress.

"We are counting first and foremost on stability in trade relations with the US," Helena Melnikov, chief executive of the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DIHK), told the broadcaster ARD television. "No more zigzagging."

Trump's repeated tariff announcements, reversals and changes to implementation deadlines have made it harder for German exporters to plan.

Melnikov said reliability in Germany's biggest export market was "extremely important," but cautioned against predicting President Donald Trump's next economic moves.

She urged Germany to expand trading partnerships beyond the US and implement promised domestic economic reforms.

Achim Wambach, president of Germany's ZEW economic research institute, warned that losing his congressional majorities could push Trump to pursue more of his agenda through trade and foreign policy, where he retains extensive powers.

"Uncertainty about the future direction of US trade policy remains high," he said, also warning of potential deadlock over the US budget.

Wambach said Democratic control would probably not bring a fundamental return to free trade, pointing to broad bipartisan agreement on protecting US industry and trade policy toward China.

Skip next section German auto industry confidence jumps

German auto industry confidence jumps

Confidence in Germany's auto industry has risen sharply, reaching its highest level since mid-2024, according to the Munich-based Ifo institute.

The survey was conducted in October, so it does not reflect the US midterm election results or their potential impact on trade policy.

Ifo's business climate index climbed from minus 33.2 to minus 4.1 points. Companies' assessment of their current situation turned positive for the first time since mid-2024, while expectations improved but remained negative overall.

"There can be no talk of an all-clear for the automotive industry," Ifo industry expert Anita Wolfl said, pointing to sharp monthly fluctuations in business confidence as evidence of considerable uncertainty.

Wolfl said a Franco-German agreement on a joint automotive strategy may have helped lift sentiment, but offered only temporary relief.

"It does not change the industry's central challenge of catching up with the leaders in technological competition," she said.

Skip next section Vonovia warns against Berlin housing takeover plans

Vonovia warns against Berlin housing takeover plans

Germany's housing group Vonovia has criticized plans by Berlin's prospective governing coalition to bring large private housing portfolios into public ownership.

The socialist Left Party, Greens and center-left Social Democrats (SPD) have agreed during coalition negotiations to target companies owning more than 10,000 apartments. Their plan envisages compensation of no more than €16 billion ($18 billion) for 160,000 homes — an average of €100,000 each.

"The plans to bring private companies' apartments into public ownership naturally concern us," Vonovia CEO Luka Mucic said while presenting quarterly results.

He called the proposal "simply the wrong approach" and legally questionable, arguing that it would create no additional housing and undermine confidence in investment.

The Financial Times estimated Vonovia's Berlin properties were worth €20.4 billion, compared with potential compensation of €12 billion.

But Maximilian Fuhrmann, a housing researcher at the German Tenants' Association in North Rhine-Westphalia, disputed that assessment. Using Vonovia's stock market valuation and debt, he calculated an average value of just over €100,000 per apartment across its portfolio — broadly in line with the proposed compensation.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

You join us as German businesses express hope that the outcome of the US midterm elections will bring a little more predictability to trade relations.

With Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress, business leaders have a simple message: "No more zigzagging."

And with the US being Germany's biggest export market, there's a lot at stake.



Meanwhile, there's some surprisingly good news from Germany's struggling car industry.

After a prolonged period of pessimism, confidence among German automakers has jumped to its highest level since mid-2024.

Stay with us here for these stories and more of what Germany is talking about today.

entries.title: Indonesia deploys troops to Jakarta after wiretapping allegations
entries.summary: Indonesian troops are being stationed in Jakarta amid wiretapping allegations implicating the president's chief of staff. Suspects are being accused of illegally tapping the president's phones.
entries.content:
Indonesia

Indonesia deploys troops to Jakarta after wiretapping allegations

November 4, 2026

Indonesian troops are being stationed in Jakarta amid wiretapping allegations implicating the president's chief of staff. Suspects are being accused of illegally tapping the president's phones.

Indonesia's military deployed more than 20,000 troops and personnel to the capital city Jakarta after authorities launched an investigation into an alleged wiretapping operation targeting the President Prabowo Subianto.

Some 20,000 troops have been deployed in Jakarta amid the scandal with the president's chief of staff is currently being investigated.

Senior military figures implicated

So far, three senior police generals have been detained. They are being accused of illegally tapping the phones of the president, journalists, politicians and business people.

Among those detained is Listyo Sigit Prabowo — not related to the president — who was the national police chief before becoming the president's chief of staff last month.

The presidential palace claims the alleged wiretapping targeting President Subianto could be regarded as an act "tending towards treason."

The authorities did not officially confirm that the deployment is connected to the scandal.

The number of troops and personnel deployed to the capital since Monday surpassed 20,000 as of Wednesday, according to the navy operations assistant, Vice Admiral Yayan Sofiyan.

Indonesian armed forces spokesperson Major General Muhammad Nas claimed that the troop movement was a "standart procedure" for maintaining national security.

Motive yet to be established

According to Indonesia's senior minister for legal affairs, the government has yet to determine the motive for the wiretapping.

The suspects, who have not responded publicly to the allegations, could face unlawful surveillance related charges, which can lead up to 10 years in prison.

"There is a strong suspicion that the wiretapping was carried out not in the interests of the state or the National Police, but for the interests of other parties,” Adrianus Meliala, a criminologist at the University of Indonesia and a former commissioner of the National Police Commission said.

"No one expected Listyo Sigit Prabowo to be named a suspect,” said Meliala, "But if the allegations are proven, the case could be understood in the context of political maneuvering. Anyone who engages in politics must also be prepared to face the political consequences," Meliala said.

entries.title: US midterms: Democrats win House and Senate from Republicans
entries.summary: The Democratic Party gained control of the House and Senate, delivering a stinging rebuke to US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. Follow DW's live updates.
entries.content:
United States of America

US midterms: Democrats win House and Senate from Republicans

Published November 3, 2026last updated November 4, 2026

The Democratic Party gained control of the House and Senate, delivering a stinging rebuke to US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. Follow DW's live updates.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Democratic Party candidates secure control of the US Senate and House of Representatives
  • Trump says Democrats 'did a good job' in midterm elections
  • Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race to become first Muslim senator in US history
  • James Talarico wins Democrats' first Senate seat in Texas in decades
  • Annie Andrews stuns Republicans in South Carolina
  • Democrats also notch wins in gubernatorial contests in Ohio and Georgia

Follow the latest developments from the US midterm elections:

Skip next section Live election results

Live election results

Skip next section German foreign minister hopes for more US support for Ukraine

German foreign minister hopes for more US support for Ukraine

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul believes the outcome of the US midterm elections could create new momentum for supporting Ukraine in its fight against Russia's military aggression.

"As far as Ukraine is concerned, I am somewhat confident that there will now be more discussions in Congress — including between both parties — about what can be done together to support Ukraine," Wadephul said in Berlin.

"I believe that people there held back for a certain amount of time during the election campaign, and I know that there are strong supporters of Ukraine in both houses and in both parties."

Wadephul stressed that foreign policy played a key role in the elections.

On US-Germany relations, he noted that bilateral cooperation could become broader and "perhaps more interesting in certain areas."

Finance Minister and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil also congratulated Democrats for what he called a "landslide victory."

"That certainly inspires confidence," he said.

For a long time, he noted, the trend had been toward right-wing populism, but now the moderate center has prevailed.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: What US midterm elections mean for Ukraine, Iran and elsewhere

IN DEPTH: What US midterm elections mean for Ukraine, Iran and elsewhere

While most foreign policy decisions ultimately rest with the executive branch, the outcome of the US midterms will have major repercussions for adversaries such as Iran, as well as countries like Ukraine, which rely on support from the United States.

Read our full report of how Tuesday's elections in the United States will likely affect other nations here.

Skip next section AfD's Weidel attributes Republicans defeats to Iran war's 'considerable consequences'

AfD's Weidel attributes Republicans defeats to Iran war's 'considerable consequences'

German right-wing populist AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel told the t-online news website that, though midterm losses for parties in power are the norm in the United States, "the extent of the Republican defeat is notable and can be best explained with the considerable consequences of the Iran war." 

She said one frequent and loud campaign promise from 2016, 2020 and 2024 had come home to roost in 2026.

"Trump promised his voters not to conduct and interventionist foreign policy," she said. "This broken promise has now come back to haunt the Republicans."

Weidel said it was in both Europe's and Germany's interests to bring the war in Iran — but also the war in Ukraine — to an end as quickly as possible.

The politician, whose party tends to be quite closely aligned with Trump's MAGA movement and some of its core backers like Elon Musk, has made no public social media comments on the vote. Instead, her comments to "t-online" focused mainly on public protests over the weekend in some cities, which she linked to "militant left-wing extremists, migrant mobs, and organized crime families."

Skip next section Iran's Qalibaf says US voters said 'no to war'

Iran's Qalibaf says US voters said 'no to war'

The speaker of Iran's parliament, Mohammad Qalibaf, who is also the country's chief negotiator in the stalled talks with the United States and intermediaries, has celebrated the result online — saying that, whatever their main motivators were, US voters had ultimately spoken out against the war in the Middle East.

"Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," he wrote on social media. "If the US [government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."

He did not elaborate on this vague threat, after several tense months of relative inactivity in the military and diplomatic standoff.

Meanwhile, a written statement was published on the website of Iranian supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei saying that anybody expecting a shift in US policy after the vote was "seriously mistaken."

"Those who still harbor even the slightest hope that the behavior of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken," the statement said.

Khamenei was severely wounded in the US strikes at the start of the war that killed his father and much of his family. He has not been seen or heard in public since amid conflicting reports about his medical and physical status, but written statements attributed to him appear periodically.

Skip next section China calls vote an 'internal matter,' Russia says it won't impact Ukraine stance

China calls vote an 'internal matter,' Russia says it won't impact Ukraine stance

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told reporters that the midterm elections were an "internal matter" for the United States. 

She said China remained willing to work with the US government to implement agreements reached by the countries, strengthen communication and manage differences appropriately.

Chinese President Xi Jinping made a high-profile state visit to the US to meet with Donald Trump amid this year's UN General Assembly, which he did not attend. While the pair tried to put on an amicable show, very little of substance emerged from the visit beyond an agreement to extend a temporary tariff truce in their trade spat for a few more weeks.

There has also been speculation about a possible trialteral meeting between Trump, Xi, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, but for now nothing has been formally arranged or announced. 

In Moscow, meanwhile, state news agency RIA cited Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov as saying he planned to wait for the final results.

"The Democratic Party leadership's approach to relations with Russia is sharply negative. There is nothing new about that," Ryabkov said. He said it would not impact Russia's position regarding its invasion of Ukraine, as the Trump administration continues to push for peace talks, albeit only arranging working-level negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv as yet.

"Our principled and consistent line regarding Ukraine — as well as our foreign policy in general — is not based on short-term considerations, and, naturally, does not depend on the fluctuations of the political barometer in other countries," Ryabkov said.

Skip next section A night of historic firsts in US elections

A night of historic firsts in US elections

Tuesday not only ushered in a series of changes in the US Congress, but it also saw a number of historic firsts in elections across the country.

Abdul El-Sayed will become the first Muslim US senator when he is sworn in next January after winning in Michigan. His win came nearly 20 years after the election of Keith Ellison to the House of Representatives. Ellison was the first Muslim elected to that body.

After defeating Trump ally Vivek Ramaswamy, Amy Acton is set to become the first female governor of Ohio.

In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black female governor of any state, as well as Georgia's first black governor, by beating billionaire Rick Jackson.

Another historic gubernatorial race took place in New Mexico, where Deb Haaland became the first Indigenous American elected to that state's highest office. Haaland is a member of the Laguna Pueblo tribe and was US secretary of the interior under former President Joe Biden.

At the same time, Ojibwe lawmaker Peggy Flanagan became the first Indigenous woman elected to the US Senate. After years in public service at the state level, she wil now represent Minnesota in Washington.

And in New Hampshire, Chris Pappas was also elected to the Senate, where he will be the first openly gay man to serve. In Alabama, Allison Montgomery became the first transperson elected to the state legislature, beating a Republican who repeatedly verbally attacked her for being trans.

More history is likely to be made in January if Hakeem Jeffries, considered the current frontrunner as minority leader, becomes speaker of the House of Representatives, as he would be the first Black man to hold that position.

Skip next section European politicians react to the 'powerful political signal' out of US

European politicians react to the 'powerful political signal' out of US

Left-leaning Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who has repeatedly clashed with Donald Trump in the past year and who faces snap elections himself at the end of the month, said Americans "voted against the policies that only impoverish," such as hate, machismo, climate denialism and the privileges of the elites. 

He drew parallels to Brazil's presidential election and the early vote he called, facing a legislative deadlock with his minority government in Spain. 

"It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain," Sanchez wrote. "The ultra wave that [Alberto Nunez] Feijoo and [Santiago] Abascal are trying to ride is no longer growing: it is crumbling."

French Finance Minister Roland Lescure reminded BFM TV that even after losing control of Congress, Trump would remain in charge on the vast majority of US foreign policy issues, and seemed to warn that the president might not prove the type to favor compromise and collaboration.

Lescure said, "Either he decides to rise above the fray, acknowledging that changes are necessary," particularly on issues like gasoline prices and his foreign policy, "or he does not." Lescure said this would be something "we will need to keep an eye on in the coming days."

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store told Reuters news agency it was a "powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters." He said voices were emerging in US politics that "are closer to us than the president and the administration have stood for, for example on climate and environment, and in foreign policy and development aid policy."

The co-leader of Germany's Green Party, Franziska Brantner, said the result was a "stop sign towards Trump and his billionaires." She said that while this pointed to "hope" for the US democratic system "hopefully getting back on its feet," it was too soon to breathe a sigh of relief in the European Union.

"On the contrary, we must really bet on Europe and on our own strengths," Brantner said. She said Trump had made it clear that he did not respect the EU and wanted to divide it, and that he wanted less and less to do with supporting Ukraine. "That means, we have our own responsibility for ourselves, no matter what the final result."

Christel Schaldemose, a European Parliament vice president from Denmark, said she was "cautiously optimistic" on Europe's behalf.

"Not because everything will now change for the better, but because it could benefit support for Ukraine, the green transition, and relations with the rest of the world," she said. But she also added that the EU must continue its course of standing on its own two feet, saying "that's not up for debate."

Skip next section Ramaphosa sees 'new era' after Democratic wins

Ramaphosa sees 'new era' after Democratic wins

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the Democratic sweep of Congress could usher in a "new era in world relations" after voters dealt Donald Trump a major electoral setback.

"The Democrats have taken control of the Senate and of the House, and the people of America have spoken," Ramaphosa told reporters. "I do think that this is going to introduce a new era in world relations."

Relations between the United States and South Africa have deteriorated under Trump. During a televised Oval Office meeting in May 2025, he confronted Ramaphosa with misleading footage and news clippings promoting false claims of a genocide against white South Africans. Ramaphosa repeatedly sought to rebut the allegations.

The Trump administration has also cut aid, expelled South Africa's ambassador and, this week, moved to end the country's duty-free access to the US market under the African Growth and Opportunity Act from January.

Ramaphosa said South Africa would continue trading with the US while seeking new export markets.

"Diversification has now become the order of the day," he said.

On Wednesday, South Africa is holding local elections of its own. 

Skip next section WATCH: Sweeping Democrat wins deliver rebuke to Trump

WATCH: Sweeping Democrat wins deliver rebuke to Trump

Democrats have scored stunning victories in states long considered Republican strongholds, flipping key Senate seats.

Brandon Bohrn, a US political analyst with the Bertelsmann Stiftung, analyzes the election results for DW.

Skip next section RECAP — Democrats claim control of Congress, flipping several Senate seats

RECAP — Democrats claim control of Congress, flipping several Senate seats

Welcome to our coverage of the US midterm elections, particularly if you're outside US time zones and were tucked up in bed as the poll-closing drama unfolded overnight. Here's the lay of the land stateside in what's now the early hours of the morning-after the vote which many saw as a referendum on President Donald Trump. 

The Democrats have fared better than polls predicted, at least based on what should now be reliable projections. They have comfortably taken control of the House of Representatives and claimed a majority in the upper chamber of Congress, the Senate. 

In a major blow for the Donald Trump administration, they have swung at least seven of the 35 Senate seats up for grabs — in North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine. Some of those states were Republican-held for decades; Kansas' two Senate seats had been reliably Republican since before World War II. 

Counting in the House races is slower, with all 435 seats up for grabs, but the Democrats have already passed the post to win the majority of the chamber with the better part of 100 seats yet to be called.

These results should markedly strengthen the Democrats' hand in Congress, giving them the power to block legislation (if perhaps not executive orders directly from President Donald Trump) and launch investigations into Trump's administration. In the Senate, they will be able to block his appointees as judges or for senior roles in government.

Trump himself praised the Democrats in an interview on Fox News on election night, saying he thought they did a "good job" and "fought hard."

"I don't view it as a hit on me," he said, despite having urged voters to act as if his name was on the midterm ballots during the campaign.

Skip next section Democrats claim majority of US governorships

Democrats claim majority of US governorships

Democrats have won a majority of US governorships for the first time in two decades, capturing offices long held by Republicans in Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Georgia.

The gains give the party more power at the state level to challenge President Donald Trump's policies on immigration, voting rules and the deployment of National Guard troops.

Several victories have also made history:

  • Georgia: Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms has become the first Black woman elected governor in the US, defeating Republican billionaire Rick Jackson
  • Texas: Gina Hinojosa has defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott to become the state's first Latina governor, despite being outspent five-to-one on advertising
  • New Mexico: Deb Haaland, a former US interior secretary, has become the first Native American woman elected governor

In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton defeated biotech billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy, describing it as "the honor of my lifetime." The victory came after a bitter campaign in which Ramaswamy's use of Acton's estranged mother in an attack ad drew widespread criticism.

In Iowa, state auditor Rob Sand thanked voters for his victory over Republican Zach Lahn. Preliminary results put Sand around 12 percentage points ahead in a state Trump won by roughly 13 points in 2024.

Republicans have held Florida, where Congressman Byron Donalds defeated David Jolly, a former Republican who ran as a Democrat.

The results could also shape the next presidential election. Governors influence election administration, while three Democrats considered potential presidential contenders in 2028 — Pennsylvania's Josh Shapiro, Illinois' JB Pritzker and Maryland's Wes Moore — have won reelection.

Skip next section DW Washington bureau chief: Results are 'more than a setback' for Republicans

DW Washington bureau chief: Results are 'more than a setback' for Republicans

The midterm election results are "more than a setback" for Republicans and President Donald Trump, DW's Washington bureau chief Ines Pohl said.

The results represent "a dramatic loss of political power" for Trump's Republican Party, she said.

See her full analysis here:

Skip next section WATCH: Republicans react to historic defeat in Texas Senate race

WATCH: Republicans react to historic defeat in Texas Senate race

DW spoke to Republican supporters at an election watch party in Austin, Texas, after Democrat James Talarico won the Senate race in the state, breaking a 38-year drought for his party in the Republican stronghold.



Skip next section German leaders congratulate Democrats, stress foreign policy power remains with the Trump administration

German leaders congratulate Democrats, stress foreign policy power remains with the Trump administration

Metin Hakverdi, who serves as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coordinator of transatlantic cooperation, said he expects the US midterm results to significantly impact the political situation between Berlin and Washington.

"America has chosen change," he told news agency DPA, while stressing that Trump remains largely in charge of foreign policy and that Germany will continue to reach out to both parties.

"We must especially not limit our contacts to individual political camps," he added, while also highlighting the historic significance of the first Indigenous woman being elected governor of New Mexico and the first black woman as governor of Georgia.

Hakverdi, a Social Democrat, has extended family in the United States and attended high school there.

Defense Minister Boris Pistorius congratulated Democrats on what he called their "historic victory." He also emphasized that the White House will remain the same and Berlin will continue to cooperate with it.

entries.title: Hungary opens communist-era secret police files identifying informants
entries.summary: The archives name thousands of former informants who spied on citizens for the state security services during decades of one-party rule. The prime minister said "many families will now face difficult information."
entries.content:
November 4, 2026

The archives name thousands of former informants who spied on citizens for the state security services during decades of one-party rule. The prime minister said "many families will now face difficult information."

Hungary released thousands of communist-era secret police records to the public on Wednesday as part of the country's long-delayed effort to come to terms with its repressive past.

The archives, which are now part of a searchable online database, include the names of thousands of former informants who worked for the state security apparatus during four decades of one-party rule.

Although communism ended in Hungary in 1989, attempts to open the files had been repeatedly stalled. Some critics blamed the delay on successive governments' reluctance to implicate public figures.

Historic move 36 years after transition to democracy

Center-right Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who unseated longtime populist leader Viktor Orban in April, had pledged to grant the public unrestricted access to the records.

"After 36 years, we are finally fulfilling what was once one of the key promises of the 1990 regime change — a promise that was later denied and lied about," Magyar told a media briefing at the state security archives on Wednesday.

He said ​some 60,000 ‌names had been made public in the new online database. A second batch of files is expected to be made available by February.

"I ask ‌everyone ​to treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity ... as many families will now face difficult information often related to a deceased member of their family," Magyar said. "​It is impossible to process a trauma without discussion and asking questions."

Coming to terms with totalitarian past

Hungary was under one-party communist rule from 1949 to 1989.

As was the case in a number of Eastern European countries during the Cold War, secret police in Hungary relied on a vast network of informants to monitor citizens. These informants were often coerced into reporting on colleagues, friends and even relatives.

According to estimates from the state security archives, authorities recruited some 150,000 informants, although records for about two-thirds of them no longer exist.

Many files were destroyed in 1956 during Hungary's anti-Soviet uprising, or hidden during the transition to democracy. Some are believed to have been taken to Moscow.

'Better late than never'

Historian Laszlo Eorsi from the 1956 Institute Foundation told the AFP news agency that the move to make the files public was "better late than never."

"We are getting access to much more information than before about who the authorities have recruited and how the security apparatus worked back then," he said.

He predicted the release would trigger public and private revelations, saying it "could cause some hysteria in the coming months."

Ahead of the publication, rumors had circulated that Former Prime Minister Orban was an informant, but his name did not appear in the digital database on Wednesday.

Orban said on Tuesday that communist secret services had tried to recruit him while he was doing his military service, but he refused.

entries.title: Wawira Njirum, Kenya's school feeder and German Africa Prize recipient
entries.summary: From a small fundraiser to a major enterprise, Wawira Njiru's Kenyan school feeding scheme has been more successful than she ever thought possible. She's now being awarded the German Africa Prize.
entries.content:
November 4, 2026

From a small fundraiser to a major enterprise, Wawira Njiru's Kenyan school feeding scheme has been more successful than she ever thought possible. She's now being awarded the German Africa Prize.

From starting a modest fundraiser for 25 school children, Wawira Njiru, 35, has become a social entrepreneur with a staggering 6,000 staff on her payroll, feeding 600,000 kids in Kenya every day with her organization Food4Education (F4E), an engagement for which she is being honored with this year's German Africa Prize. How did this transformation come to pass?

The answer may be in her character. Stubborn and hardworking, that's how Njiru sees herself. "It's hard to tell me something is not possible."

Thinking back to how she began, she explained, "My dream then, my ambition was to feed 100 kids every day. I was 21 years old then, so also having an ambition of feeding 100 kids felt momentous. But now growing up, but also figuring out that you can do more, and just being obsessed with 'How much more can you do? How much more can you do?' led me here."



Njiru left her native Kenya after finishing school to study nutrition science in Adelaide, Australia.

Connecting the dots

"I knew a lot of kids back home were not getting the education they needed. At that time, I was learning about the impact of food, and I didn't realize how powerful food was," Njiru said.

"When you're doing a nutrition degree, that's when you really learn about the science behind food. And knowing that, especially for kids, it's so critical that they get nutritious meals."

When she found out her friends at the university often had a few dollars to spare and were looking for ways to contribute, she connected the dots and started her first fundraiser.

From there, the trajectory was set. But the road was rough at times for the young woman she was, Wawira explained. Some people didn't take her seriously. Others did.

"You have to find your believers," Njiru found out. "You can't just go with your own name. You have to find someone to vouch for you or someone or something to validate your presence."

Her degree certainly helped. But still, many men looking for jobs just didn't seem confident in working for a young woman. This is why more than 70% of her employees today are women, Njiru said.

School meals at 3 cents, digitally tracked

Steadily pushing the limits, Food4Education now provides 19,000 schools across Kenya with more than 600,000 meals every day. The system relies on a mix of funding: through donations and government funding, parents are left with a small contribution, which in some cases amounts to 5 Kenyan shillings (3 US cents).

Payment is processed through the so-called "Tap-to-Eat" system. Every child has a wristband that is used to track each meal. The wristbands not only track parents' payments, but they also help document how many meals are actually served. And if children don't pick up their meals, the team can find out why.

The model also relies on local sources wherever possible. About 80% of the food the organization distributes comes from small-scale farmers. This way, school meals are freshly sourced — and farmers have a reliable market for selling their produce.

"For a long time, school meals were viewed as charity. We've proven that it's economic infrastructure," Njiru said.

Boosting attention and morale among school children

Does it pay out? It seems so. Data show that children at participating schools miss fewer classes, and they also perform better at school.

"Food is everything," said Raphaera Kanya, director of a primary school in Kenya's capital Nairobi. "When your stomach has nothing, you cannot understand anything in class."

To Jane Nyambura, a pupil, the school feeding fosters equality at school.

"There was a difference because there are some students who are finding accessing food very easy because their parents are available," she told DW.

"There are others who can't afford food, and they feel as if it's unfair, as if there's something lacking in them. So it really demoralizes them and reduces their confidence."

Njiru has already set her sights on the next benchmark: Reaching 1 million schoolchildren every day. She has every right, it seems, to be confident.

"From 25 kids to now, I feel like there's not one challenge that we haven't overcome."

The Prize is awarded by the German Africa Foundation (DAS), a nonpartisan foundation dedicated to promoting a nuanced view of Africa in political circles and among the German public.

Since 1993, it has awarded the German Africa Prize to individuals from African countries whose ideas and work inspire solutions to global issues of the future beyond their countries of origin. The award has gone to outstanding individuals in Zimbabwe, Cameroon and Sierra Leone in recent years.

German Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan will present the  German Africa Prize to Kenya's successful social entrepreneur on Wednesday evening.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: BMW reports lower Q3 earnings as China woes mount
entries.summary: BMW reports a drop in profits in the July to September quarter amid fierce competition from China.
entries.content:
November 4, 2026

BMW reports a drop in profits in the July to September quarter amid fierce competition from China.

German carmaker BMW reported a nearly 15% drop in third-quarter net profit on Wednesday, as competition from China shakes the global car industry.

Net profit for the third quarter fell to 1.45 billion euros ($1.61 billion), while sales fell nearly 6% to 30.45 billion euros, BMW said.

The main cause of the decline was BMW's poor business in China. Although the company sold more cars in the US and Europe compared to the same period last year, this could only partially offset the decline in China.

BMW's car deliveries in China, which were already at their lowest level since 2017 last year, fell 24.8% in the quarter and consequently dragged global deliveries down by 6.3.

CEO Milan Nedeljkovic said his company would "specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures."

BMW on Tuesday also lowered its outlook for the current year, citing the faster-than-planned implementation of restructuring measures that includes 8,000 layoffs in its home market.

Germany's auto industry struggling because of weak demand and competition from China

German carmakers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market,  resulting in cost-cutting measures.

Volkswagen, the world's second-largest carmaker, is battling mounting competition from falling demand in its core Chinese market.

BMW, and its industry heavyweight peers, Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.

The Volkswagen Group posted its worst quarterly results in more than a decade earlier this October.

It is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW has announced that it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.

On the other hand, German auto parts supplier Schaeffler announced on Tuesday that it planned to cut almost 3,500 jobs and close five sites in Europe, by 2028.

According to the company statement, three-fourths of the 3,460 job cuts and four of the five site closures will be in Germany.

German automotive supplier Bosch, the world's biggest, announced last year that it would cut 13,000 jobs, mostly in its auto division.

entries.title: Germany's celebrated children's author Janosch has died
entries.summary: Bear, Tiger and Tiger-Duck: The author and illustrator Janosch achieved world fame with his heartwarming children's figures. He died at the age of 95.
entries.content:
November 4, 2026

Bear, Tiger and Tiger-Duck: The author and illustrator Janosch achieved world fame with his heartwarming children's figures. He died at the age of 95.

Janosch, the pen name of German author and illustrator Horst Eckert, won hearts around the world with his warm and simple sense of humor. He charmed children and adults alike with his iconic Tiger, Bear, Tiger-Duck and other animals. 

Janosch created more than 150 books, which have been translated into over 30 languages.

His best-selling children's book, "Oh, wie schön ist Panama," translated into English as "The Trip to Panama," was so lucrative that Janosch was able to settle down on the Canary Island of Tenerife in 1980, where he lived together with his wife Ines. The writer and illustrator died peacefully at the age of 95, his publisher Bernhard Feil announced on Wednesday.

Dismissed from arts school

Janosch was born as Horst Eckert on March 11, 1931, in Hindenburg (now Zabrze, Poland) in what was then Upper Silesia. After World War II, his family had to flee to Germany.

In 1953, Janosch started studying at the Academy of Art in Munich, thinking that it would be easy to become an artist. He was however dismissed after just a few terms for "lack of talent."

But luckily for his later readers, Janosch did not give up. He continued to work as a freelance artist, soon discovering his second great gift, namely writing.

His first children's book about a horse named Valek was published in 1960.

Although Janosch became famous primarily for his children's books, he also wrote books for adults that focused on his own childhood.

The dream of a beautiful childhood

Even though he wrote cheerful books for children, Janosch hardly had any positive memories of his own childhood, as his father was an alcoholic. He was beaten not only by him but also by his mother and grandmother. Raised in a strictly Catholic environment, he was continuously threatened to be punished by God.

Later on, Janosch tried to overcome the burden of his childhood memories by turning to alcohol as well.

He always expressed a great deal of understanding for children, trying to encourage them to stand up for their rights. As a result of his childhood experiences, Janosch did not want to have children himself, and his attitude towards the Catholic Church always remained divided. "As I am a sinner and a heretic, God will let me live a long life so that I can return to the Church," he told his biographer Angela Bajorek.

Janosch's animal figures are endearing but not always well-behaved. They love all kinds of nonsense. But even if they lie to each other or put their own interests first, the true winner at the end of stories is always friendship and solidarity.

Janosch's path towards world fame

Janosch achieved his major breakthrough with "The Trip to Panama," a story about two friends, a little tiger and a bear, who set out to find their paradise in Panama. After touring around in circles, they finally end up where they started out; they realize that their journey was the destination. Janosch received the German Youth Book Prize in 1979 for the work.

Janosch's protagonists have become familiar to generations of children all over the world. They come up over and over again in the various stories carefully illustrated with water colors.

There is the honest lion Hans from the toy chest who fails to catch a nutcracker with his lies. There is Schnuddel and a ridiculous bragger Günter the Box-Frog. And then there is a tiger that collects mushrooms while looking out for his devoted friend, a bear, who always stands up for him even when the tiger temporarily leaves him because of a little pig in one of the stories.

Merchandising with a Tiger-Duck

The "Tigerente," literally "Tiger-Duck," a wooden duck on wheels with yellow-brown stripes, appears on numerous pictures by the illustrator. At times, the animal has been tossed into a corner, at times it is hanging from the ceiling, or the Box-Frog pulls it across the drawing.

His iconic figures, especially the Tiger-Duck, have served as motifs on various items, from cups to stamps to jewelry, and even on airplanes. Film adaptations and TV series based on his stories were produced in German and English.

'He who needs almost nothing, has everything'

Guests who visited Janosch in Tenerife were impressed by his very modest lifestyle. He always said that hanging around in his hammock doing nothing was what he enjoyed most. And yet Janosch remained very active until the end of his life.

From 2013 to 2019, he wrote a column for the German weekly Die Zeit, taking on the role of Mr. Wondrak, who commented on world affairs. Shortly before his 90th birthday in 2021, the complete collection of his Mr. Wondrak columns were published as a book in German.

Like the protagonists in his stories, Janosch always tried to content himself with few things. As he wrote in one of his books: "He who needs almost nothing, has everything."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: South Africans vote in local elections in test for ANC
entries.summary: Failing public services, corruption and high crime rates have led to growing frustration among South African voters. That could lead to further losses for the ANC.
entries.content:
South Africa

South Africans vote in local elections in test for ANC

November 4, 2026

Failing public services, corruption and high crime rates have led to growing frustration among South African voters. That could lead to further losses for the ANC.

South Africans began voting Wednesday in municipal elections that could lead to fresh losses for the African National Congress (ANC).

The party of Nelson Mandela, which has led the country since the end of apartheid, has seen its popularity fall over the past decade.

In the previous local elections in 2021, it won less than 50% of the vote for the first time, and polls suggest it could drop below 40% this time.

Wednesday's vote is taking place amid rising frustration over failing public services, including unreliable water and electricity supplies, high crime rates, unemployment, and affordable housing. Concerns about undocumented migration also featured prominently in some campaigns.

The elections — seen as a gauge of public mood before national polls in 2029 — will decide who leads South Africa's eight main cities as well as 44 district municipalities and 205 local councils.

Battle for Johannesburg

A crucial battleground is the city of Johannesburg. The economic hub is currently governed by a fragile ANC-led coalition, but polls suggest the liberal Democratic Alliance (DA), South Africa's second-biggest party, could win the most votes there.

The DA has put forward former national leader Helen Zille as candidate for Johannesburg mayor. The DA is also expected to retain control in the city of Cape Town.

Other closely watched areas include Tshwane, home to the administrative capital Pretoria, and the port city of Durban, where former President Jacob Zuma's MK party is mounting a strong challenge.

Voters do not directly elect mayors but choose municipal councillors, who then choose the mayors and form administrations that will run cities.

Declining ANC popularity

Although the ANC still has a loyal supporter base due to its role in ending apartheid, a growing number of South Africans are fed up with persisting problems such as high unemployment, power cuts and water shortages.

"Municipal failures have contributed to declining public trust and confidence ​in democratic governance," said President Cyril Ramaphosa, who acknowledged failures within his party, but also voiced optimism: "This election is an opportunity to turn this around."

The ANC lost its 30-year parliamentary majority in national elections in 2024, forcing it to enter into a national coalition with the DA and several other parties.

A further decline in the ANC's popularity at a local level could mean several cities will be ruled by unstable coalition governments.

More than 29 million citizens are registered to vote. But in the last municipal elections in 2021 less than half of them cast ballots.

Polls close at 9 p.m. local time (1900 GMT) and results are expected on Sunday.

entries.title: What US midterm elections mean for Ukraine, Iran and elsewhere
entries.summary: Donald Trump's Republicans will no longer control the US Congress after the Democrats flipped both chambers in the midterm elections. The outcome could impact conflicts in Europe and the Middle East.
entries.content:
United States of America

What US midterm elections mean for Ukraine, Iran and elsewhere

November 4, 2026

Donald Trump's Republicans will no longer control the US Congress after the Democrats flipped both chambers in the midterm elections. The outcome could impact conflicts in Europe and the Middle East.

The outcome of the midterm election will shape policy in the United States for years and have repercussions around the globe. Decisions made in Washington affect both US adversaries such as Iran and countries such as Ukraine, which is seeking more US support.

President Donald Trump does not have the final say when it comes to deciding where the United States goes to war or which countries get financial or military aid. While the president wields more power in the US than in parliamentary democracies such as Germany, he does not govern alone — even in the land of opportunity.

The House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers of Congress in which the Democratic Party secured a clear majority on Tuesday, wield considerable influence. They decide on legislation and government spending and also serve as a check on the president and the intelligence agencies.

The president can veto legislation passed by Congress. Congress can override that veto with a two-thirds majority in both chambers. The legislature also handles impeachment proceedings. In addition, the president can only appoint Cabinet members, US ambassadors and federal judges from a list of nominees the Senate approves.

In the 2024 US election, the Republican Party secured not just the White House through Trump's reelection but also both chambers of Congress, which made it easier for the US president to govern.

The Democrats' resounding midterm victory has now flipped control of both chambers, which could shift the direction of major foreign policy issues.

Ukraine may see little benefit from Democrat wins

Joe Biden, a Democrat, was in the White House when Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine. Alongside Europe, the US stood out as a reliable partner, supporting Ukraine with financial aid, military expertise and, above all, large-scale weapons deliveries.

The situation changed abruptly under Trump. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy  famously received a notably frosty welcome during his 2025 visit to the White House. Trump now openly admits that he gets along better with Russian President Vladimir Putin than with Zelenskyy.

The US has suspended sanctions against Russia and reduced financial and military aid to Ukraine. Now the Democrats have majorities in both chambers of Congress, they could put increased support for Ukraine on the agenda.

"Democrats criticize the Trump administration for not doing enough for Ukraine," Brandon Conradis, a former DW journalist and now an editor at Bloomberg Government, told DW before Tuesday's election. "They can push legislation that would provide more aid to Ukraine."

If Trump vetoed such legislation, the outcome would depend on the balance of power in Congress. But a two-thirds majority could override his veto with support from some Republicans.

Can Democrats end the Iran war?

Trump launched the war against Iran alongside Israel on February 28, 2026, without consulting Congress. Under the US Constitution, Congress must approve a formal declaration of war against another country. Democrats have repeatedly voted against the war and even passed a resolution, together with some Republicans, calling for an end to the hostilities. The Trump administration has ignored it.

"I don't think Congress will have huge powers here," said Michael O'Hanlon, director of research for foreign policy at the US think tank Brookings Institution, told DW before the midterm elections, but added that Congress could perhaps prevent a major escalation by refusing to fund it.

How the midterms could impact US development aid

US support for aid projects around the world that help fight Ebola, AIDS and hunger was sharply cut back by President Trump shortly after he began his second term. Among other measures, he shut down USAID, the US agency responsible for foreign development assistance.

Whether a Democratic-controlled Congress could "reactivate" the agency against the president's wishes is questionable. But Congress could push for increased aid spending and investigate the controversial closure of USAID.

"Democrats would have oversight power and use it to scrutinize the closing of USAID," Conradis said. "There will be hearings, and they will drag officials they view as responsible in front of Congress."

Ultimately, the US remains a country with a Republican president. There will be no complete reversal, of course. "It's not like if Democrats win control of Congress, everything is going to change. But some things will change because the power dynamics will be different."

This article was originally published in German on November 3, 2026. It was updated on November 4, 2026, to reflect the outcome of the midterm election.
